record.notes: USD 28 a year divided by 12 is USD 2.33 a month, which is the vendor's own figure, and USD 28 is the money out of pocket. This is above the USD 1 line and is recorded because it is the cheapest verified machine that needs no shared address and no port forwarding at all. A WireGuard listener on UDP 51820 works on any port here because the IPv4 is dedicated. Payment: the USD 1 authorisation is real and first-party, but it is a card-verification fee placed when a card is added, not a signup deposit, and it is refunded automatically within 7 days rather than on request. The money actually spent on the plan is non-refundable. Whether the signup flow itself requires a card was not established: the account creation form was not opened, and the help-centre articles describe the billing profile after an account exists. RENEWAL PASS 2026-10-24: the annual figure is the standing product price, not a promo, so the renewal is the same USD 28 absent a notified increase. the provider do permit that increase at the start of a renewal term on 45 days' notice, and the agreement auto-renews for the same term unless cancelled at least one day before expiry. The two SSD VPS records now carry the same renewal treatment; the SSD VPS 1 record previously left renewal_usd null while SSD VPS 2 carried it, although both are priced the same way on the same page.

free_tier.stated: Still trading, but the reason to record it is a data-loss incident rather than a price: several Los Angeles host nodes were compromised through a Virtualizor vulnerability, the boot sectors of affected guest disks were overwritten with a ransom note, and the vendor states that the data on those disks cannot be recovered. The vendor's own wording, reposted in the forum: 攻击者损坏了与VPS相关的磁盘，磁盘上的数据无法恢复.

record.chaining: This is the reason any free or cheap host among evaluated providers needs a second copy elsewhere: the composition that survives an incident is two providers plus an object store, not one provider plus its own snapshots.
record.limits_note: What fails is durability: a hypervisor-level compromise destroyed guest disks across several nodes and the vendor confirmed non-recovery, so a snapshot kept on the same provider is not a backup.
record.binding_note: What fails is durability: a hypervisor-level compromise destroyed guest disks across several nodes and the vendor confirmed non-recovery, so a snapshot kept on the same provider is not a backup.
